name: NeuralPath VaultPay Subdermal Transaction Node
body_location: subdermal palmar — dominant hand, metacarpal region between index and middle finger base
description:
The VaultPay is a subdermal payment and identity node implanted in the metacarpal web of the dominant hand, positioned so that a natural forward extension of the hand — the gesture used to offer a handshake or tap a surface — activates the near-field transaction broadcast. The implant contains an encrypted financial ledger shard linked to the user's registered Meridian Civic Account, capable of processing standard quanta-denominated transactions through any NFC-compatible payment terminal, transit gate, vending unit, or access panel in the city. Unlike earlier-generation payment chips implanted in the wrist, the VaultPay's palmar placement is optimized for natural gesture activation, reducing false triggers from incidental contact. Security is handled through a dual-layer system: a passive biometric pulse confirming the user's cardiovascular signature, and a subvocally-confirmed transaction PIN for purchases above a user-set threshold.

By 2200, the subdermal payment chip is arguably the single most common implant in GLMZ — more ubiquitous than even sleep optimizers. The city's transit system, most retail infrastructure, and all corponation campuses require or strongly prefer implant-based authentication. Carrying physical tokens or an external device for payment marks a person as either very old, very poor, or a tourist. The VaultPay specifically targets Tier 1–3 users with competitive pricing and a straightforward civic account integration that doesn't require a corporate employment contract to activate. For Shelf residents, the VaultPay also functions as a de facto identity document for city services, food subsidy programs, and emergency medical identification — making it something that social workers and civic aid organizations actively push for homeless and transient populations to receive through subsidized programs.
installation_requirements: Pharmacy kiosk or walk-in clinic; 15-minute outpatient procedure under local topical anesthetic; no specialist required; same-day activation
maintenance: No physical maintenance required; security firmware updated automatically via encrypted OTA push; annual account re-verification recommended; unit is rated for 20-year lifespan

side_effects: Mild warmth at the implant site during high-frequency transaction periods (e.g., busy market days)
Occasional phantom activation sensation — a faint buzz in the palm — when passing near high-density NFC fields such as transit hubs
Some users develop habitual hand gestures or fidgeting around the implant site during the adjustment period
Rare cases of minor localized swelling in the first two weeks post-installation
cultural_context: The subdermal payment chip is so normalized in GLMZ that its absence is the thing that gets noticed. Not having a payment implant — relying on a physical card, a wearable, or worse, token currency — reads as poverty, eccentricity, or deliberate off-grid ideology depending on context. On the Shelf, subsidized VaultPay programs distributed through civic aid centers are genuinely life-changing: access to food subsidy terminals, transit gates, and city services is effectively gated behind implant authentication in most districts. There is a persistent criminal ecosystem around stolen or cloned payment chip signals — called 'skinlifting' or 'ghost tapping' — though NeuralPath's cardiovascular biometric lock has made this significantly harder than it was with earlier generations. Political dissidents and privacy advocates sometimes have their chips 'cold-sleeved' — wrapped in a bioelectric dampening sheath that requires manual removal to activate — as a protest against surveillance infrastructure that uses ambient payment chip pings to track pedestrian movement through the city.
known_users: Virtually all GLMZ residents across Tiers 1–4
Civic aid recipients and Shelf residents accessing subsidy programs
Migrant workers and new arrivals to the city seeking civic integration
Transit workers and service industry employees for whom fast authentication is a daily necessity
Privacy advocates with modified or shielded units as a political statement
story_hooks: A 'ghost tap' attack has been hitting Shelf-district residents — someone has developed a way to spoof the cardiovascular biometric lock on older VaultPay units, draining accounts in passing; the victims are too poor to absorb the loss and too low-tier for corporate security to prioritize, so they're coming to the characters.

A civic aid worker discovers that the subsidized VaultPay units distributed to homeless populations have a secondary firmware package logging location data at 30-second intervals — the data is being sold to a real estate corponation mapping 'undesirable foot traffic' to accelerate Shelf-district rezoning.

A character's VaultPay begins triggering phantom transactions — small amounts, Ψ1–Ψ3, draining to an unregistered account — and the transaction logs show the payments happening while the character is asleep, suggesting either a sophisticated remote exploit or that someone has a near-perfect clone of their biometric signature.
